Replacing Turf in Lake Nona's Earliest Villages

Turf replacement in Lake Nona is quoted per job once the old surface and base are assessed, not by a flat per-foot rate, as of September 2026. The community's earliest phases, dating to the years after Lake Nona's population passed 1,500 residents in 2000, are old enough that first-generation synthetic turf there may already be nearing the end of its service life.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

First-generation turf meets a new material standard

Any synthetic lawn installed in Lake Nona's earliest built phases went in before Florida 2026 turf standard existed, which means it was never required to meet the current rule's limits on heavy metals, added PFAS or infill type. A replacement project today has to meet that standard regardless of what the original installation used, so a homeowner swapping out a decade-old lawn is effectively upgrading the material spec at the same time as the surface itself, not just replacing like for like. That is worth knowing before assuming a straight swap is possible, since a crumb-rubber infill common in an older install no longer fits the state's rule for a home lawn outside a playground's footprint.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older Lake Nona lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

The base often needs correcting, not just the surface on top

A first-generation turf lawn nearing replacement age has usually spent a decade or more compacting the base underneath it, and Lake Nona's sandy flatwoods soil, with a water table that rises close to the surface for stretches of the year, does not forgive a base that has settled or lost its ability to drain. Pulling the old turf is the point where that base gets a real inspection, since a replacement laid over a settled or fines-clogged base just repeats whatever drainage problem the original install had. How long a system should last in the first place is covered in this piece on turf lifespan in Florida.

Swapping old crumb rubber for a compliant infill

A Lake Nona lawn or general play area installed years ago sometimes has crumb rubber or another synthetic infill spread across the whole yard rather than confined to equipment fall zones, which was common before the current rule limited rubber and other synthetic infill strictly to the ground under playground equipment. Replacement is the point where that infill gets swapped for clean silica sand, zeolite, or a coated sand across the open lawn area, while rubber stays only where equipment actually sits. This is one of the more common corrections we make on an older lot during a full re-turf.

Say you have a 720 sq ft original-phase Laureate Park lawn ready for replacement

A 720 sq ft lawn from Laureate Park's earliest build-out, showing matted pile and a base that no longer drains evenly, is a realistic replacement candidate given how long the community has been established. Replacement is quoted per job once the crew sees the base condition, but for planning purposes, a new installation at that size in the $8–$18 range would run roughly $5,800 to $13,000, with base correction adding to that figure if the old subgrade needs rebuilding rather than just re-leveling. Because the original lawn predates the 2026 material standard, the new infill and backing have to meet today's rule even if nothing about the footprint changes.

Scheduling a rebuild around the rainy season's compaction window

Base material compacts properly only when it's reasonably dry, so a Lake Nona replacement scheduled during the June-through-September rainy season needs tighter weather windows than the same job in a drier month, sometimes splitting demo and base work across a few days to catch dry stretches between afternoon storms. A replacement planned for the dry season has more flexibility, which is one reason timing a full tear-out and rebuild around the calendar, not just around a homeowner's availability, affects how smoothly the job actually goes.

An irrigation line capped with tape instead of properly sealed

A sprinkler line simply folded over and taped rather than cut back and capped with a proper fitting is a common shortcut on a Lake Nona replacement, and tape doesn't hold against water pressure the way a sealed cap does. A line that fails this way months later can undermine the new base from below with a slow, hidden leak, the kind of problem that's invisible until a soft spot appears in turf that's only been down a short time. Confirming each line was properly capped, not just covered, is worth asking about directly.

Design review again, even for a lawn that already exists

Swapping an existing synthetic lawn for a new one sounds like maintenance rather than a design change, but Laureate Park's standards treat any modification different from the original approved plan as something the Design Review Board should see again, and a replacement that changes color, pile height or footprint from what is on file qualifies. A true like-for-like replacement is a smaller ask than a first-time installation, but it is worth confirming with the association before assuming no paperwork is needed, a step the HOA packet checklist walks through either way.

A second full year comparison, not just the first rainy season

Watching a Lake Nona replacement through its first rainy season catches the most obvious settling issues, but a second full year, covering a complete dry season and wet season the lawn hasn't been through yet, reveals slower changes that only show up once new infill and base material have had a full annual cycle to compact and shift. A deliberate comparison against day-one photos at that two-year mark, rather than assuming the lawn stopped changing after its first several months, catches a gradual drift the earlier check would have missed entirely.

Questions people ask

Does a straight turf replacement in Laureate Park need a new HOA application?

A true like-for-like swap is a lighter ask than a first install, but any change in color, pile height or footprint from what is on file should go back to the Design Review Board before work starts.

Can old crumb-rubber infill be reused when replacing a Lake Nona lawn?

Not on an open home lawn. The state's 2026 standard limits infill there to silica sand, rock, shell or coated sand, and reserves rubber or other synthetic infill for the footprint of playground equipment only.
